question: What proportion of adult inpatients have their drug allergy status recorded using one of the three standard categories (drug allergy / none known / unable to ascertain) before their first drug is prescribed?
why: Unclear or missing allergy status is a recurrent cause of prescribing error and delayed antibiotic administration. No closed-loop audit of the specific three-category recording standard has been published in the library, although related allergy-documentation audits exist [1892].

standard.wording: Document people's drug allergy status in their medical records using 1 of the following: 'drug allergy' 'none known' 'unable to ascertain' (document it as soon as the information is available).

pass: One of the three standard categories is recorded in the drug chart or EPR allergy field before the first drug is administered
population: Inclusion: 40 consecutive adult medical or surgical admissions. Exclusion: patients transferred from another ward with allergy status already recorded there and unchanged.
sample: 40 consecutive adult admissions over the last 4 weeks
data_source: Drug chart or EPR allergy field, admission clerking note

question: What proportion of adults treated in hospital for suspected anaphylaxis are offered a referral to a specialist allergy service before discharge?
why: Adult referral after anaphylaxis is under-audited in the library; existing entries cover children [see NNA-188] and adrenaline auto-injector supply [see NNA-085], leaving the adult referral step unmeasured.

standard.source: NICE NG258 Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment, rec 1.1.12 (2011, updated 2026, replaces CG134)
standard.wording: After emergency treatment for suspected anaphylaxis, offer the adult, young person or child a referral to a specialist allergy service (age-appropriate, where possible) consisting of healthcare professionals with the skills and competencies necessary to accurately investigate, diagnose, monitor and provide ongoing management of, and patient education about, anaphylaxis.

pass: A referral to a specialist allergy service is documented as offered (accepted or declined) in the discharge letter
population: Inclusion: adults (16 and over) treated for suspected anaphylaxis in the emergency department or on a ward. Exclusion: patients who die before discharge.
sample: 30 consecutive adults over the last 6 months (from anaphylaxis coding or adrenaline administration records)
data_source: ED/ward notes, discharge summary, adrenaline administration record used to identify cases

question: What proportion of adults treated for anaphylaxis who receive a single dose of adrenaline with a good response are observed for at least 2 hours before discharge, and what proportion needing two or more doses are observed for at least 6 hours?
why: The minimum safe observation period after anaphylaxis has never been separately audited in the library; existing entries focus on tryptase timing [see NNA-084] rather than the length of observation itself.

standard.source: NICE NG258 Anaphylaxis: assessment and referral after emergency treatment, recs 1.1.7 and 1.1.8 (2026)
standard.wording: A suitably qualified and experienced healthcare professional should consider discharging the adult, young person or child after 2 hours of observation... if there was a good response (within 5 to 10 minutes) to a single dose of intramuscular (IM) adrenaline... Observe the adult, young person or child for a minimum of 6 hours after resolution of all symptoms if: 2 doses of intramuscular (IM) adrenaline were needed to treat the anaphylaxis or there is a history of biphasic reaction.

pass: Documented observation time meets or exceeds the 2-hour (single good-response dose) or 6-hour (two or more doses, or biphasic history) minimum before discharge
population: Inclusion: adults treated for suspected anaphylaxis with at least one dose of IM adrenaline. Exclusion: patients admitted to a ward or critical care rather than discharged from the assessment area.
sample: 30 consecutive cases over the last 6 months
data_source: ED observations chart, drug chart (adrenaline doses and times), discharge time

Clinic time pressure can make same-visit printing impractical → agree realistic clinic template time with the service before cycle 1
Patients who prefer a digital copy should still be offered one, recorded as an equivalent pass
pearls: Combine this audit's data collection with the driving-discussion audit, since both use the same clinic letters
Ask reception or clinic support staff to print and hand over the plan at check-out, taking pressure off clinicians
Offer an electronic copy via the patient portal as an alternative to a paper copy
Use patient feedback (a short survey) to confirm plans given were actually understood, not just handed over
effort: ~10 min per 10 patients from clinic letters

question: What proportion of women and girls with epilepsy of childbearing potential have a documented discussion of the risks of their anti-seizure medication in pregnancy within the last 12 months?
why: This measures the broader pregnancy-risk discussion for any anti-seizure medication, distinct from the valproate-specific Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form audits already in the library [see NNA-159, NNA-186, NNA-323].

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 4.3.7 (2022)
standard.wording: Discuss with women and girls with epilepsy who are able to have children (including young girls who are likely to need treatment when they are able to have children), and their families or carers if appropriate, the risks to an unborn child of taking antiseizure medications during pregnancy, such as congenital malformations, neurodevelopmental impairments and fetal growth restriction.

pass: A documented discussion of pregnancy risks of anti-seizure medication within the last 12 months in the clinic letter
population: Inclusion: women and girls of childbearing potential (12 and over) with epilepsy under active neurology or paediatric neurology follow-up. Exclusion: women who have had a permanent sterilisation procedure documented.
sample: 30 consecutive women/girls of childbearing potential on the epilepsy clinic caseload
data_source: Epilepsy clinic letters from the last 12 months

template.note: local pseudonymised ID, never the real hospital number

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a mandatory annual 'pregnancy risk of current anti-seizure medication discussed' field to the epilepsy clinic letter template for all women and girls of childbearing potential.
reaudit: 12 months after the mandatory field is added, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at neurology governance; keep the mandatory field if the target is met.
evidence: [159 nearest related entry: two-specialist sign-off for valproate under 55; 323 nearest related entry: Annual Risk Acknowledgement Form for repeat valproate]
pitfalls: This applies to all anti-seizure medications, not only valproate, so existing valproate-specific systems will not fully capture it → build a medication-agnostic field
Young girls not yet needing contraception discussions may still need age-appropriate risk information → include this group explicitly, not just adult women
Discussions at GP-led reviews (rather than specialist clinic) may be missed if only specialist letters are checked → clarify which setting is in scope before cycle 1
Patients seen only by telephone may have shorter, less complete documentation → check both face-to-face and telephone clinic letters
pearls: Use the same clinic caseload list as any existing valproate ARAF audit to avoid duplicating case-finding work
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse, who often leads these discussions in practice
Provide clinicians with a short structured prompt card covering all anti-seizure medications with teratogenic risk, not only valproate
Report findings by medication class to show where risk communication is strongest and weakest
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters

question: What proportion of people of childbearing potential prescribed an enzyme-inducing anti-seizure medication (carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or topiramate) have documented advice about reduced hormonal contraceptive effectiveness?
why: Interaction advice for enzyme-inducing anti-seizure medications and hormonal contraception is a distinct recommendation from the valproate-specific pregnancy prevention audits already in the library, and is not measured anywhere.

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 4.3.10 (2022)
standard.wording: Be aware that some antiseizure medications, for example, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin and topiramate, can impair the effectiveness of hormonal contraceptives. Refer to the summary of product characteristics (SPC) and BNF or BNF for children for individual drug advice on the interactions between antiseizure medications and contraception.

pass: Documented advice about reduced hormonal contraceptive effectiveness and the need for an alternative or additional method
population: Inclusion: people of childbearing potential prescribed carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, phenytoin or topiramate for epilepsy, under active follow-up. Exclusion: patients using a copper intrauterine device or another method unaffected by enzyme induction, if already documented.
sample: 30 consecutive eligible patients on the epilepsy clinic caseload
data_source: Epilepsy clinic letters, GP contraception review records

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add a drug-interaction alert to the epilepsy prescribing system that fires when one of the four enzyme-inducing medications is prescribed to a person of childbearing potential, prompting a documented contraception discussion.

pitfalls: This standard covers four specific drugs, not all anti-seizure medications, so the alert must be drug-specific to avoid unnecessary prompts
Contraception method may be managed entirely in primary care and not visible to the neurology clinic → check both GP and specialist records
Non-hormonal or copper IUD users need this explicitly recorded as 'not applicable' rather than being marked as a fail
Topiramate's own separate Pregnancy Prevention Programme requirements (already audited) may overlap with this general interaction advice → keep the pass criteria distinct
pearls: Coordinate with the existing topiramate Pregnancy Prevention Programme audit to avoid double data collection on the same patients
Provide a simple interaction quick-reference card (drug name, effect on contraception, alternative advice) for clinicians
Recruit a contraception/sexual health lead as an occasional co-reviewer for complex cases
Report by individual drug, since carbamazepine, phenytoin, oxcarbazepine and topiramate caseloads may differ in size
effort: ~15 min per 10 patients from clinic letters

question: What proportion of people with epilepsy who continue to have seizures despite treatment are offered an epilepsy specialist nurse session after each emergency department attendance for a seizure?
why: Epilepsy specialist nurse contact after an ED attendance is a specific, checkable recommendation not currently measured by any audit in the library.

standard.source: NICE NG217 Epilepsies in children, young people and adults, rec 11.1.3 (2022)
standard.wording: For people with epilepsy who continue to have seizures, offer epilepsy specialist nurse sessions: at least twice a year and after emergency department visits.

pass: An epilepsy specialist nurse contact (session, call or clinic appointment) is documented within 2 weeks of the ED attendance
population: Inclusion: people with known epilepsy and ongoing seizures who attend the ED with a seizure over the last 6 months. Exclusion: ED attendances for a reason unrelated to epilepsy in a person who happens to have the condition.
sample: 30 consecutive epilepsy-related ED attendances over the last 6 months
data_source: ED attendance record, epilepsy specialist nurse contact log

timeline: Wk 1–2 collect; Wk 3 analyse/present; Wk 4 change; Wk 5–12 embed; Wk 13–14 re-audit
change: Add an automatic epilepsy specialist nurse referral to the ED discharge system, triggered whenever a seizure-related attendance is coded in a patient with known epilepsy.
reaudit: 6 months after the automatic referral is switched on, same template, same sample size
close_loop: Present at the joint ED/neurology governance meeting; keep the automatic referral if the target is met.
evidence: [no audit of epilepsy specialist nurse contact after emergency department attendance has been published in the library]
pitfalls: ED coding may not clearly distinguish a seizure-related attendance from other reasons → cross-check with the triage complaint as well as the diagnosis code
Epilepsy specialist nurse capacity may not match ED attendance volume → agree a realistic response model (call-back, not always a face-to-face session) with the service before cycle 1
Attendances out of hours or at weekends may be harder to flag for follow-up → build the referral into the discharge process itself, not a manual daily list
Patients who decline contact should be recorded as offered but declined, not as non-compliance
pearls: Base the automatic referral trigger on the same seizure-related attendance coding used for existing seizure audits
Recruit the epilepsy specialist nurse team directly, since they are best placed to say what response is realistic
Track whether ED re-attendance rates change over time as a secondary outcome of better specialist nurse contact
Present this alongside the referral-to-first-seizure-clinic audit for a fuller picture of the epilepsy urgent care pathway
effort: ~15 min per 10 attendances from ED/specialist nurse records
